Right: its eight spanning trees as miniatures in two rows, in the order the iterator yields them, with each tree's edges in the accent color, the unused edges dashed and its total weight underneath: 6, 7, 8, 9 on the top row and 9, 10, 10, 11 below. The first, A–B, B–C, C–D, is the minimum spanning tree." width="100%"} `minimum_spanning_tree()` finds the single cheapest tree. This method keeps going: it yields the cheapest spanning tree, then the second cheapest, and so on, one at a time and only as far as you iterate (with `minimum=False`, from heaviest to lightest). Every spanning tree is produced exactly once, so exhausting the iterator lists them all, but the point of the ordering is that you can stop early: - the `k` best alternatives to the MST, for robust or multi-criteria network design (rank by cost, then pick the best tree that also meets a constraint the MST ignores) - the cheapest tree with a property that is hard to optimize directly, such as a bounded degree or diameter: iterate until a tree passes the test - ranking explanations of tree-structured data by likelihood As with `minimum_spanning_tree()`, edge direction is ignored, self-loops are never used and parallel edges count as different trees. `include=` and `exclude=` restrict the iteration to the trees that use every included edge and none of the excluded ones. The iterator works on a snapshot of the edges and weights taken when it is created. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [minimum]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), yield trees from lightest to heaviest; if `False`, from heaviest to lightest. [weight_attr]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Name of the edge attribute to use as the weight. If `None` (the default), each edge's weight field is used (`1.0` on an unweighted graph), as it is for `"weight"`. Under any other name, every edge must hold a number. [include]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges every tree must contain, as edge IDs or `(u, v)` node pairs (a pair stands for every edge between the two nodes, in either direction). [exclude]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [list | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edges no tree may contain, given the same way. [return_subgraphs]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [bool]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [[True]{.va}]{.doc-parameter-default} : If `True` (the default), yield a new `Graph` per tree, with every node of the original and the tree's edges. If `False`, yield the tree's edges as `(source_id, target_id, weight)` tuples, which is much cheaper. ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [Iterator[Graph] or Iterator[list[tuple[int, int, float]]]]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The spanning trees in order of total weight. Ties between equally heavy trees come out in a fixed order. When no tree satisfies the constraints, nothing is yielded; an empty or single-node graph yields one tree without edges. ::: ## Raises {.doc-raises} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [ValueError]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : If the graph is disconnected (it has no spanning tree), an edge value is NaN, an edge is both included and excluded, an edge or node pair in `include=` or `exclude=` does not exist, or `weight_attr=` names an attribute that an edge lacks or holds as a non-number. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} Sörensen and Janssens (2005) partition the set of spanning trees. A partition is the set of trees that contain some included edges and avoid some excluded ones, and its cheapest tree comes from Kruskal's algorithm run on the included edges first. After a partition's tree $T$ is yielded, the rest of the partition is split on the open edges $e_1, \dots, e_k$ of $T$: part $i$ includes $e_1, \dots, e_{i-1}$ and excludes $e_i$. Every other tree of the partition lies in exactly one part, so a priority queue of parts keyed by their cheapest tree yields all trees in order, each once. Each tree costs at most $V - 1$ Kruskal runs, $O(V E)$ time after the edges are sorted once. This is NetworkX's `SpanningTreeIterator`. ## Examples {.doc-examples} A weighted square with one diagonal has eight spanning trees. Their weights, in order: ::: {#d3d8f898 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec g = ec.Graph(weighted=True).add_nodes(["A", "B", "C", "D"]) g.add_edges( [("A", "B", 1.0), ("B", "C", 2.0), ("C", "D", 3.0), ("D", "A", 4.0), ("A", "C", 5.0)] ) [ sum(t.get_edge(e).weight for e in t.get_edge_ids(limit=None)) for t in g.iter_spanning_trees() ] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` [6.0, 7.0, 8.0, 9.0, 9.0, 10.0, 10.0, 11.0] ``` ::: ::: The iterator is lazy, so taking the three cheapest trees doesn't enumerate the rest: ::: {#42695776 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} from itertools import islice for tree in islice(g.iter_spanning_trees(), 3): print(sorted(tree.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True))) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ['A--B', 'B--C', 'C--D'] ['A--B', 'B--C', 'D--A'] ['A--B', 'C--D', 'D--A'] ``` ::: ::: Here the best tree whose nodes all have degree at most 2 (a Hamiltonian path) is the first one that passes the test: ::: {#db469f7f .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} best_path = next( t for t in g.iter_spanning_trees() if max(t.get_degree(n) for n in "ABCD") <= 2 ) sorted(best_path.get_edges_str_repr(use_labels=True)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=3} ``` ['A--B', 'B--C', 'C--D'] ``` ::: ::: Constraints restrict the iteration. Only two trees use the diagonal and avoid A-B; with `return_subgraphs=False` each comes as `(source_id, target_id, weight)` tuples, here summed to the tree's weight: ::: {#3d799056 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} trees = g.iter_spanning_trees( include=[("A", "C")], exclude=[("A", "B")], return_subgraphs=False ) [sum(w for _, _, w in edges) for edges in trees] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ``` [10.0, 11.0] ``` ::: :::
